title: 1 Timothy 1:3–11
context: Paul reminds Timothy why he remained at Ephesus: to command certain men not to teach a different doctrine or lose themselves in myths and endless genealogies. The aim of the charge is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and sincere faith; the law is good when used lawfully, and sound doctrine accords with the gospel of the blessed God’s glory.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: The charge at Ephesus, love from a pure heart, and the lawful use of the law: older Arminian and Reformed writers, each in their own words.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: Charge some to teach no other doctrine—Than I have taught. Let them put nothing in the place of it, add nothing to it. The end of the commandment—of the whole Christian institution—is love. The foundation is faith; the end, love. But this can only subsist in an heart purified by faith, and is always attended with a good conscience. We grant the whole Mosaic law is good, answers excellent purposes, if a man use it in a proper manner.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (on 1 Tim 1:3–11)

reformed.quote: The sum of the law is this, that we may worship God with true faith and a pure conscience, and that we may love one another. Thus we must begin with faith, and not with love. Paul acknowledges that the law is good, but contends that we are required to make a lawful use of it. He maintains that the law of God was given in order to restrain the licentiousness of wicked men; because they who are good of their own accord do not need the authoritative injunction of the law.

verses.text: As I urged you when I was going into Macedonia, stay at Ephesus that you might command certain men not to teach a different doctrine,
verses.arminianNotes:
Timothy is to remain and command certain men not to teach a different doctrine. The deposit is the apostolic gospel, not a private hobby of the teacher.

Arminians hear both authority and responsibility: the church must refuse additions and replacements, and teachers can actually swerve. Grace enables Timothy to stay at his post; it does not make the charge optional.
verses.reformedNotes:
Paul arms Timothy with a charge, not a suggestion. Remaining at Ephesus is apostolic strategy for a church in danger of novelty.

God guards the gospel through appointed means—a clear command, a faithful deputy, and the refusal of rival teaching. The church is not a marketplace of doctrines; it lives by the one gospel entrusted to the apostle.

verses.text: and not to pay attention to myths and endless genealogies, which cause disputes rather than God’s stewardship, which is in faith.
verses.arminianNotes:
Myths and endless genealogies breed speculation instead of building up God’s household in faith. Curiosity can crowd out trusting Christ.

God’s household is ordered through faith—a living, sincere trust, not pedigree puzzles. Teachers and hearers must not devote themselves to what displaces the gospel they are called to believe.
verses.reformedNotes:
Paul tests teaching by its fruit: speculations versus God’s stewardship, which is by faith. Useless questions do not edify, however ancient they sound.

The economy of God is received by faith, and faith itself belongs to the gospel God gives. Rival curricula are not harmless extras; they unseat the stewardship God has appointed.

verses.text: But the goal of this command is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and sincere faith,
verses.arminianNotes:
The aim is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and sincere faith. Wesley: the foundation is faith; the end is love—and love only lives in a heart purified by faith.

Arminians insist that sincere faith is the living condition of this love. The charge is not for controversy but for a purified people who actually love God and neighbor.
verses.reformedNotes:
Love is named first, yet it springs from faith. Calvin: we must begin with faith, not with love; God purifies the heart by faith, and a good conscience rests on Christ.

Unfeigned faith, clean conscience, and love are the law’s true sum—and they are the fruit of the gospel, not a ladder of self-made virtue.
verses.keyContrast: Both name love from a pure heart, good conscience, and sincere faith as the charge’s aim. Arminians typically treat sincere faith as the grace-enabled condition from which love issues and must be kept; Reformed commentators often treat faith, conscience, and love as gifts the gospel produces, beginning with faith God works.

verses.text: from which things some, having missed the mark, have turned away to vain talking,
verses.arminianNotes:
Certain persons swerved from love, conscience, and sincere faith into vain discussion. The path can be left.

An itch for impressive knowledge distances a person from faith and the sense of divine things. Empty disputes are not a side hobby; they are what remains when the heart leaves the aim of the charge.
verses.reformedNotes:
They missed the mark and turned to idle talk. Paul judges doctrine by edification: what does not build up in faith is vanity, however admired.

When the fear of God cools, the tongue still works—only now it multiplies questions that cannot save. Vain discussion is a symptom of having left the gospel’s end.

verses.text: desiring to be teachers of the law, though they understand neither what they say nor about what they strongly affirm.
verses.arminianNotes:
They want the status of law-teachers without understanding their words or subject. Confidence is not competence.

Pastoral Arminian note: the law is holy, but mishandled law becomes a platform for pride. Teachers remain accountable for what they assert; grace does not baptize ignorance that harms the flock.
verses.reformedNotes:
Paul rebukes not open enemies of the law but those who claim its chair. Rashness loves to pronounce on what it does not know.

Ambition plus the law’s vocabulary is an old snare. Sound teaching requires both true matter and a humble form—not confident assertions about shadows.

verses.text: But we know that the law is good if a person uses it lawfully,
verses.arminianNotes:
The law is good if used lawfully. Wesley grants the Mosaic law excellent purposes when properly used: the ceremonial points to Christ; the moral convicts unbelievers and guides believers in holiness.

Arminian readers refuse both antinomianism and law as a ladder of merit. Used well, the law serves the gospel that establishes it rather than competing with it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Paul will not let opponents paint him as burying the law. The law is good—and it must be used as law, in agreement with the gospel he preaches.

Lawful use means the law does its God-appointed work, not the work of justifying sinners. The gospel of glory does not erase the law; it puts the law in its place.

verses.text: as knowing this, that law is not made for a righteous person, but for the lawless and insubordinate, for the ungodly and sinners, for the unholy and profane, for murderers of fathers and murderers of mothers, for manslayers,
verses.arminianNotes:
The law is not laid down as a weapon against the just—those justified by faith and walking in love—but it does address the lawless and disobedient. It names rebellion: ungodliness, violence, contempt of parents, murder.

Pastoral reading: the law still tells the truth about sin so that sinners might be convicted and driven to the Savior, not so teachers can win arguments.
verses.reformedNotes:
Paul views the law in reference to people: it restrains the licentious. Those who aim at good from the heart are not the law’s targets in this polemic; the lawless are.

Zeal for the law that never strikes at actual wickedness is a hollow shield. God gave the law to name and curb sin, and the gospel agrees with that verdict.

verses.text: for the sexually immoral, for homosexuals, for slave-traders, for liars, for perjurers, and for any other thing contrary to the sound doctrine,
verses.arminianNotes:
The catalog continues into sexual immorality, same-sex practice, enslaving others, lying, and perjury—plus whatever else contradicts sound doctrine. These are; they are ways of harming neighbor and defiling the conscience.

The gospel calls such sinners, as it called Paul, to repentance and faith. Sound doctrine is healthy teaching that does not relabel these as harmless.
verses.reformedNotes:
Paul groups sins against body, liberty, and truth, then gathers “for any other thing contrary to the sound doctrine.” Healthy teaching and this catalog are not rivals.

The gospel of glory does not make light of what God names as sin. It saves sinners from these things and trains a people to refuse them—without turning the vice list into a substitute gospel.

verses.text: according to the Good News of the glory of the blessed God, which was committed to my trust.
verses.arminianNotes:
All of this accords with the Good News of the glory of the blessed God, entrusted to Paul. The gospel does not void the law; it establishes the law’s true end in Christ.

The entrusted gospel is for proclamation—the glory of God announced so that hearers may believe. Timothy’s charge is to keep that gospel from being swapped for speculation.
verses.reformedNotes:
Paul calls it the gospel of glory because in it God displays His glory. He says it was entrusted to him so that no rival “good News” of fables can claim equal standing.

Comfort: there is one glorious gospel of the blessed God. The apostle’s trust is a stewardship of that gospel, not a license to invent.
